label: Sixteen Mahajanapadas
summary: Buddhist lists name sixteen large states, among them Magadha, Kosala, Kashi, Avanti and Gandhara. The lists are textual and the exact date of the political map is approximate.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (600 BCE); Wikipedia, 'Vedic period' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period>, accessed 2026-11-22 (consolidated by 6th c. BCE)

label: Keezhadi urban settlement
summary: Excavations near Madurai uncovered brick buildings and Tamil-Brahmi potsherds. Reported radiocarbon dates reach c. 6th century BCE and are still debated.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Licchavi republic of Vaishali
summary: Vaishali was governed by an assembly of clan heads rather than a king, one of the early ganasanghas known from Buddhist and Jain texts. The period is approximate.
source: Romila Thapar, Early India (2002), general survey; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Bimbisara of Magadha
summary: Bimbisara is remembered as an early king of Magadha who made Rajagriha his capital and grew the state by alliance and conquest. Regnal dates differ between Buddhist and Jain lists.
source: R. C. Majumdar (ed.), History and Culture of the Indian People, dynastic chronology; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Mahavira nirvana (traditional date)
summary: Jain tradition places the liberation of Mahavira, the last teacher of this age in Jainism, in 527 BCE. Modern historians often prefer a date about a century later.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (527 BCE); Jain tradition

label: Persian rule reaches Gandhara and Hindush
summary: Inscriptions of Darius I name Gandara and Hindush among the lands he held. Parts of the north-west thus lay inside the Achaemenid empire.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Cyrus reaches north-west 538 BCE); Wikipedia, 'Vedic period' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Cyrus and Darius I, early 6th c. BCE)
flag: Wikipedia timeline puts Persian arrival at 538 BCE (Cyrus); the Darius inscriptions naming Gandara and Hindush are c. 520-518. Range stored.

label: Punch-marked silver coins appear
summary: Small silver pieces stamped with several symbols circulate widely in the Ganga plain and beyond. They show trade and the reach of early states. Start dates are debated.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Parinirvana of the Buddha (debated)
summary: Buddhist tradition says the Buddha died at Kushinagar aged about eighty. Scholars debate the year: 483 or 486 BCE on the long count, or about 400 BCE on the short one.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (proposed 483 BCE); Wikipedia, 'Ashoka' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashoka>, accessed 2026-11-22 (483 or 486 BCE derivations)
flag: Buddhist dating is debated; 483/486 BCE (long chronology) versus c. 400 BCE (short chronology).

label: First Buddhist council at Rajagriha
summary: Buddhist accounts say monks gathered at Rajagriha soon after the Buddha's passing to recite his teachings and rules. Our knowledge of it comes from later texts.
source: Pali and Sanskrit Buddhist chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa) read through modern summaries; tradition, not history. Not checked on the web.

label: Second Buddhist council at Vaishali
summary: Buddhist chronicles describe a council at Vaishali over points of monastic discipline, after which communities are said to have begun to divide. Details vary by school.
source: Pali and Sanskrit Buddhist chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa) read through modern summaries; tradition, not history. Not checked on the web.

label: Panini composes the Ashtadhyayi
summary: Panini fixes Sanskrit grammar in about four thousand compact rules, a landmark in linguistics. His date, c. 4th century BCE, is debated.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (350 BCE)

label: Nanda dynasty seizes Magadha
summary: Mahapadma Nanda is credited by Puranic and Buddhist lists with founding a large, rich realm centred on Pataliputra. The dates rest on late chronologies.
source: R. C. Majumdar (ed.), History and Culture of the Indian People, dynastic chronology; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Alexander enters the north-west
summary: Alexander of Macedon crosses the Hindu Kush and moves into Gandhara, where the ruler of Taxila makes terms. Greek writers record the campaign.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Ambhi of Takshila surrenders 326 BCE)

label: Battle of the Hydaspes
summary: Alexander meets the king Porus (Puru) on the river Jhelum. Greek sources record a hard fight, after which Porus keeps his kingdom as an ally.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (May 326 BCE)

label: Alexander's army turns back at the Beas
summary: Tired troops refuse to march further east beyond the Hyphasis (Beas). Alexander turns back and leaves governors behind in the Indus lands.
source: Greek and Roman writers (Arrian, Pliny, Periplus) via modern summaries; not read in the original. Not checked on the web.

label: Chandragupta Maurya takes Magadha
summary: Chandragupta overthrows the Nandas and founds the Mauryan state at Pataliputra. Later tradition credits the minister Kautilya as adviser. The date is approximate.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22; Thapar, Early India (recalled)
verification: web (one source) + memory; second web source needed

label: Chandragupta and Seleucus make a treaty
summary: Greek writers say Seleucus gave up eastern lands in return for a large force of elephants, and the two courts exchanged envoys. The terms are known only in outline.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (lists 305 BCE battle and 304 BCE cession); Greek writers via summaries
flag: Timeline gives 305 for the clash and 304 for the cession.
verification: web (one source) + memory; second web source needed

label: Megasthenes at Pataliputra
summary: The Greek envoy Megasthenes lives at the Mauryan court and writes about the city, its wall and its officials. His book is lost and survives only through later writers.
source: Greek and Roman writers (Arrian, Pliny, Periplus) via modern summaries; not read in the original. Not checked on the web.

label: Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions begin
summary: Short inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi script on caves and pottery are the earliest written Tamil. Their first dates are debated, c. 3rd century BCE onward.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Bindusara succeeds Chandragupta
summary: Bindusara reigns over a wide empire, and Greek sources record exchanges with the Seleucid court. Chandragupta is traditionally said to have ended his life as a Jain ascetic.
source: R. C. Majumdar (ed.), History and Culture of the Indian People, dynastic chronology; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Ashoka becomes king
summary: Ashoka succeeds to the Mauryan throne after a struggle among princes recorded in later Buddhist chronicles. His own edicts date events from his consecration.
source: Wikipedia, 'Ashoka' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashoka>, accessed 2026-11-22 ; Britannica, 'Ashoka' <https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ashoka>, accessed 2026-11-22 ; Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22. Primary: Major Rock Edicts (not read)
flag: Sources disagree: Wikipedia Ashoka c. 268-269 BCE; Wikipedia timeline 273 BCE; Britannica c. 265 or 273 BCE. Range stored.

label: The Kalinga war
summary: Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII says the conquest of Kalinga came in his eighth regnal year and brought him deep remorse. The edict is his own account, and the calendar year depends on when his reign began.
source: Wikipedia, 'Ashoka' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashoka>, accessed 2026-11-22 ; Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22. Primary: Major Rock Edict XIII (not read)
flag: Edict says 8th regnal year; calendar year depends on accession date (see Ashoka accession). Wikipedia Ashoka c. 260; timeline 265 BCE.

label: Barabar caves given to the Ajivikas
summary: Rock-cut caves near Gaya carry Ashokan inscriptions saying they were given to the Ajivika ascetics. They are among the earliest cut caves in India.
source: Ashokan edicts (Sircar; Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka); dates by regnal year, as reported. Not checked on the web.

label: Ashoka's dhamma edicts begin
summary: Rock and pillar edicts across the empire urge care for the sick, for animals and for elders, and respect for all sects. They are written in Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic.
source: Ashokan edicts (Sircar; Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka); dates by regnal year, as reported. Not checked on the web.

label: Greek and Aramaic edicts at Kandahar
summary: Edicts in Greek and in Aramaic have been found near Kandahar, showing that the Mauryan court addressed Greek-speaking and Aramaic-reading subjects.
source: Ashokan edicts (Sircar; Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka); dates by regnal year, as reported. Not checked on the web.

label: Third Buddhist council at Pataliputra
summary: Sri Lankan chronicles say a council was held under Ashoka to settle the teachings and to send teachers abroad. It is not mentioned in his edicts.
source: Pali and Sanskrit Buddhist chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa) read through modern summaries; tradition, not history. Not checked on the web.

label: Mahinda carries Buddhism to Sri Lanka
summary: Sri Lankan chronicles say Ashoka's son Mahinda taught the king Devanampiyatissa and began the Buddhist order on the island. Dates are traditional.
source: Pali and Sanskrit Buddhist chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa) read through modern summaries; tradition, not history. Not checked on the web.

label: Lion Capital of Sarnath
summary: A polished sandstone capital with four lions stood on an Ashokan pillar at Sarnath. Its mastery of stone shows the high skill of Mauryan workshops.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Great Stupa at Sanchi begun
summary: The core brick stupa at Sanchi is traditionally linked with Ashoka. The stone gateways were added later, in the Shunga and Satavahana periods.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Ashoka names Chola, Pandya and Chera
summary: Ashokan edicts name the southern neighbours as Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputa and Kerala-putra, the first record of those names in a royal text.
source: Ashokan edicts (Sircar; Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka); dates by regnal year, as reported. Not checked on the web.

label: Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini
summary: An inscribed pillar records that the king visited the birthplace of the Buddha and eased the village's taxes. It is a main proof for the place.
source: Ashokan edicts (Sircar; Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka); dates by regnal year, as reported. Not checked on the web.

label: Satavahana line in the Deccan (early)
summary: The Satavahanas rise in the Deccan after the Mauryas, with inscriptions at Nashik and Naneghat. Their early dates are debated.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Simuka c. 230 BCE)

label: End of the Mauryan line
summary: The last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, is said in later texts to have been removed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga. The Shunga line then ruled the heartland.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (185 BCE)

label: Bharhut stupa railing and gateway
summary: Carved stone panels at Bharhut tell Jataka tales and name donors in short inscriptions. They are valued as a record of early Buddhist art.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Patanjali's Mahabhashya
summary: Patanjali comments on Panini's grammar and mentions living events of his day. His date, around the 2nd century BCE, is approximate.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Menander I and the Indo-Greek kingdoms
summary: Greek-ruled kingdoms in the north-west minted fine coins with Greek and Prakrit legends. Menander is the best known and is remembered in the Pali Milindapanha.
source: Greek and Roman writers (Arrian, Pliny, Periplus) via modern summaries; not read in the original. Not checked on the web.

label: Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar
summary: An inscription on a stone pillar says that Heliodorus, an envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, set it up in honour of Vasudeva. It is early evidence of Greeks joining a Bhagavata devotion.
source: D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription
summary: A cave inscription near Bhubaneswar records the deeds of the Kalinga king Kharavela year by year, including canal works and gifts. Its date, 2nd to 1st century BCE, is debated.
source: D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Rock-cut Buddhist caves of the western Deccan
summary: Cave halls and monasteries at Bhaja, Karla and Pitalkhora are cut from the rock with donors named in inscriptions. They follow wooden building forms.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Saka rulers in the north-west
summary: Rulers of Central Asian origin, the Sakas, take over parts of the north-west under Maues and others, and leave coins and inscriptions in several lands.
source: Romila Thapar, Early India (2002), general survey; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Kanva dynasty in Magadha
summary: After the Shungas, a short-lived Kanva line holds Magadha according to Puranic lists. The record is thin and the dates are approximate.
source: R. C. Majumdar (ed.), History and Culture of the Indian People, dynastic chronology; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Vikrama era begins
summary: The Vikrama samvat counts years from 57 BCE. Tradition links it to a king Vikramaditya, but who began it, and when it was first used, is debated.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (58 BCE)
flag: Timeline gives 58 BCE; common reckoning is 57 BCE.
verification: web, sources disagree by one year, range stored

label: Indo-Parthian ruler Gondophares
summary: Coins and the Takht-i-Bahi inscription show Gondophares ruling in the north-west in the early 1st century CE. Later Christian legend links his name to a visit by an apostle.
source: R. C. Majumdar (ed.), History and Culture of the Indian People, dynastic chronology; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Kujula Kadphises unites Kushan clans
summary: Kujula Kadphises founds the Kushan realm that later spans Central Asia and north India. The start date is approximate.
source: Wikipedia, 'Kushan Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kushan_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22; Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (68 CE)
flag: Kushan page gives c. 25-85 (infobox) or c. 50-90; timeline gives 68 CE. Range stored.

label: Thomas tradition in Kerala
summary: The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala hold that the apostle Thomas brought their faith in 52 CE. The tradition is old and respected; historians cannot confirm the date.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
summary: A Greek sailors' guide lists Indian ports and goods such as pepper, cotton and pearls. Its date, 1st century CE, is debated.
source: Greek and Roman writers (Arrian, Pliny, Periplus) via modern summaries; not read in the original. Not checked on the web.

label: Pliny on the Roman trade with India
summary: Pliny the Elder writes that Rome spends large sums on goods from India. Roman coin finds in the south support the picture of a busy trade.
source: Greek and Roman writers (Arrian, Pliny, Periplus) via modern summaries; not read in the original. Not checked on the web.

label: Arikamedu and Muziris trade posts
summary: Ports on both coasts traded with the Roman world. Pottery and coins show the contact at Arikamedu, and a later papyrus records a cargo from Muziris.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Gandhara and Mathura sculpture
summary: Workshops at Gandhara and Mathura begin to carve images of the Buddha and of other figures. The styles differ and their dates and links are debated.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Gautamiputra Satakarni's reign
summary: Gautamiputra Satakarni rules the Satavahana state at its widest. His mother Gautami Balashri's Nashik inscription praises him. Dates are approximate.
source: D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Kanishka's reign begins (proposed)
summary: Kanishka rules a large Kushan realm and supports art and religion. Starting dates between 78 and 144 CE have been argued; c. 127 is one common proposal.
source: Wikipedia, 'Kushan Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kushan_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (reign from 127 CE, per Falk); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (127 CE)
flag: Era start debated: 78 CE and other dates argued; 127 CE now widely accepted (Falk). Wikipedia Kushan page does not discuss the 78 CE view; that part is from memory.
verification: web, two sources agree on 127; alternatives from memory

label: Fourth Buddhist council in the Kushan period
summary: Northern Buddhist tradition describes a council held under Kanishka. Whether and where it met is debated.
source: Pali and Sanskrit Buddhist chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa) read through modern summaries; tradition, not history. Not checked on the web.

label: Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription
summary: Rudradaman of the Western Kshatrapas records at Junagadh the repair of a lake first dug in Mauryan times. It is an early long inscription in Sanskrit.
source: D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Karikala and the Kallanai (traditional)
summary: Tamil poems praise the Chola king Karikala. Tradition links him with an early weir on the Kaveri, the Kallanai, whose first builders are not firmly dated.
source: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Natyashastra compiled
summary: The Natyashastra sets out the arts of drama, dance and music in detail. It is attributed to Bharata, and its date is debated within several centuries.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Manusmriti and the dharmashastra literature
summary: Texts on law and duty such as the Manusmriti take shape c. 200 BCE to 200 CE. Their authority and effect, and later critiques of them, are discussed widely.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Charaka and Sushruta medical compilations
summary: The Charaka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita set out early Indian medicine and surgery. Authorship is traditional and layered, and dates are debated.
source: Histories of Indian mathematics and astronomy (e.g. Joseph, Plofker); recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Bakhshali manuscript
summary: A birch-bark mathematical manuscript uses a dot for zero. Radiocarbon dates for its leaves span several centuries, and what they date is disputed.
source: Histories of Indian mathematics and astronomy (e.g. Joseph, Plofker); recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Tolkappiyam and early Tamil poetry
summary: The Tolkappiyam, a Tamil grammar, and the Sangam anthologies form the oldest Tamil literature. Their dates are debated, c. 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: The Panchatantra (traditional)
summary: Animal fables told to teach statecraft and daily conduct were gathered in the Panchatantra. It reached Persia and the West by translation. The Sanskrit text's date is approximate.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Gupta era begins
summary: A new calendar counted from 319 or 320 CE marks the accession of Chandragupta I and is used in Gupta inscriptions.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Chandragupta I coronation 26 Feb 320); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (320 CE)

label: Samudragupta's campaigns
summary: The Allahabad pillar inscription, composed by Harisena, lists the kings Samudragupta defeated or made allies. It is a rare record in praise-poem form.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (succeeded c. 335 or 350, ruled to c. 375); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22; Primary: Allahabad pillar inscription (not read)
flag: Accession 335 or 350 CE; the pillar inscription is undated.

label: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya
summary: Chandragupta II extends Gupta power to the western coast and issues fine gold and silver coins. His reign, c. 375-415, is a peak of Gupta arts.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (ruled 375-415)

label: Iron pillar at Mehrauli
summary: A rust-resistant wrought-iron pillar bears a Sanskrit inscription in honour of a king Chandra, usually identified as Chandragupta II. It is famed for its metalwork.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Faxian travels in India
summary: The Chinese monk Faxian walks through north India collecting texts and records towns, monasteries and the mild rules he sees. His stay lasts about a decade.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (left China 399, in India 405-411 CE)

label: Nalanda Mahavihara founded
summary: Seals and Chinese accounts link the start of the great monastery at Nalanda with the Gupta king Kumaragupta I. It later draws students from many lands.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (under Kumaragupta I, who ruled to 455); Chinese accounts via summaries
flag: Founding year is uncertain within the reign of Kumaragupta I; Wikipedia Gupta page gives 455.

label: Kalidasa (traditional placement)
summary: The poet and dramatist Kalidasa wrote Shakuntala, the Meghaduta and other works. He is often placed in the Gupta period, but details of his life are unknown.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Skandagupta faces the Hunas
summary: The Bhitari pillar inscription and the Junagadh inscription say that Skandagupta halted a Huna attack. The pressure on the empire continues afterwards.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Huna attack repelled c. 455; Skandagupta died 467)

label: Ajanta paintings under the Vakatakas
summary: Rock-cut halls at Ajanta are painted with scenes from Buddhist stories, in the time of the Vakataka rulers. Several caves date from this period, c. 460-480.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya
summary: Aryabhata gives rules for the movements of the sun, moon and planets and for calculation. He says the earth turns on its axis. The book is dated to 499 CE.
source: Histories of Indian mathematics and astronomy (e.g. Joseph, Plofker); recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Silappatikaram and Manimekalai
summary: These two Tamil epics tell of a merchant's wife and of a young woman who becomes a Buddhist nun. Their dates are debated, c. 5th to 6th centuries CE.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya (early structure)
summary: A brick temple stood by the Bodhi tree by the Gupta period. The standing building was heavily rebuilt in the 19th century. Early dates are debated.
source: Archaeological survey reports and museum summaries; recalled, report not read. Not checked on the web.

label: Yashodharman defeats Mihirakula
summary: A pillar inscription from Mandasor says Yashodharman of Malwa overcame the Huna king Mihirakula. Buddhist sources describe Mihirakula as harsh.
source: Wikipedia, 'Gupta Empire' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Yashodharman drove out Huns 528); Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (Battle of Sondani 528)
flag: Wikipedia timeline names the clash the Battle of Sondani; the Mandasor inscription is the primary source (not read).

label: Varahamihira's Pancasiddhantika
summary: Varahamihira summarises five older astronomical systems in the 6th century CE and writes on weather, buildings and omens. His date is approximate.
source: Histories of Indian mathematics and astronomy (e.g. Joseph, Plofker); recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Harsha Vardhana crowned
summary: Harsha takes the throne of Thanesar and Kannauj. Banabhatta's Harshacharita and Chinese records describe his court. His realm falls apart after his death.
source: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Indian history' <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Indian_history>, accessed 2026-11-22 (606 CE)

label: Xuanzang travels in India
summary: The Chinese monk Xuanzang studies at Nalanda and travels widely in India between 629 and 645. His account is a main source for the 7th century.
source: Chinese pilgrim and envoy accounts (Faxian, Xuanzang, Yijing) via modern summaries. Not checked on the web.

label: Banabhatta writes the Harshacharita
summary: The court writer Bana composes a prose life of Harsha and the novel Kadambari. They are major Sanskrit prose works. Dates c. 7th century CE.
source: Standard histories of Sanskrit, Tamil and regional literature; dates of authors often debated. Not checked on the web.

label: Aihole inscription of Ravikirti
summary: The poet Ravikirti records the victories of the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II, including a check on Harsha. It is dated 634 CE and is an early dated Kannada-country text.
source: D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions Bearing on Indian History and Civilization; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Pallava art at Mamallapuram
summary: Under Narasimhavarman I and later Pallava kings, monolithic temples and sculpted rock panels are cut at the coast. The Shore Temple follows c. 700 CE.
source: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Pallavas take Vatapi
summary: A Pallava army under Narasimhavarman I enters the Chalukya capital Vatapi after earlier defeats. Inscriptions on both sides record the rivalry.
source: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India; recalled, page not checked. Not checked on the web.

label: Chinese mission of Wang Xuance
summary: A Tang envoy reaches the north after Harsha's death and finds a disturbed realm. The episode shows the links between India and China.
source: Chinese pilgrim and envoy accounts (Faxian, Xuanzang, Yijing) via modern summaries. Not checked on the web.

label: Alvars and Nayanars: bhakti in Tamil
summary: From about the 6th to 9th centuries, singer-saints of Vishnu and Shiva compose hymns in Tamil that carry devotion into daily life. Dates of individuals are debated.

label: Arab conquest of Sindh

label: Lalitaditya of Kashmir

label: Kailasa temple at Ellora

label: Adi Shankara (traditional dates)

label: Vikramashila Mahavihara founded
